description: Data Sufficiency is a crucial part of Logical Reasoning. It tests whether the provided statements are adequate to answer a specific main question. The objective is not to calculate the exact answer, but to evaluate the sufficiency of the given information.

sections.title: Basic Concept
sections.description: The fundamental structure and requirements of Data Sufficiency questions.

key_concepts.explanation: The core problem you need to find the answer to. It can be based on any logical or mathematical topic.
Two or three sets of information provided after the question. You must check which of these contains the necessary data to answer the question.
The question must have only one definite answer. If the given information yields multiple possible answers, the data is considered insufficient.

sections.title: Standard Answer Choices
sections.description: The five standard options typically asked in examinations and their logical meanings.

results: When a definite answer is obtained using Statement I alone.
But Statement II alone fails to provide an answer.
When a definite answer is obtained using Statement II alone.
But Statement I alone fails to provide an answer.

cases.condition: Either I or II is sufficient
results: When Statement I by itself is capable of answering the question.
And Statement II by itself is also independently capable of answering the question.

cases.condition: Neither I nor II is sufficient
results: When no definite answer is obtained even after combining the information from both statements.
When neither statement alone provides the answer.
But combining the information from Statement I and Statement II yields a definite answer.

sections.title: Steps to Solve
sections.description: A systematic process to solve data sufficiency questions without making logical errors.

steps.title: Analyze the Question
steps.detail: Read the question carefully and understand exactly what is being asked (e.g., a specific direction, a relationship, or a numeric value).

steps.title: Independent Check of Statement I
steps.detail: Use only the information from Statement I. Completely ignore Statement II at this stage. Check if a definite answer is found.

steps.title: Independent Check of Statement II
steps.detail: Now use only the information from Statement II. Do not carry over any information from Statement I. Check if a definite answer is found.

steps.title: Combining the Statements
steps.detail: Only if both Step 2 and Step 3 fail to yield an answer (i.e., they are individually insufficient), you should combine the data from both statements and check again.

sections.title: Applications in Logical Topics
sections.description: How to check for data sufficiency across various logical reasoning topics.

results: Determining the gender and generation gap is crucial.
If a person's gender is unknown, their exact relationship often cannot be determined.
The exact relative position between the starting point and ending point must be known.
Providing only the distance or only the direction is usually insufficient.
To find the total number of persons, information from both ends (Left/Right or Top/Bottom) might be necessary.

sections.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
sections.description: Common errors made by students during exams that lead to incorrect evaluations.

key_concepts.explanation: Do not assume any extra information outside of what is strictly provided in the statements.
Never combine the statements until you have tested both of them independently and found them individually insufficient.
Do not waste time fully solving the problem to find the exact numerical answer; you only need to verify if the data exists to find it.
